title: The OWL Project - Education & Conservation
quickSummary: Founded in 2001, owlproject.org has reached 260,000 South African children and their families, teaching them about owls as natural pest controllers while transforming perceptions in communities. The program installs occupied owl boxes in schools and uses owl pellet dissection to contribute to scientific data analysis.
keyTakeaways: 260,000 children and parents have participated since 2001
Program demystifies negative stigma and teaches 'owls eat rats'
Awarded the Birdlife Africa Award for Conservation and International Owl Centre recognition

impact.title: Educational Impact
impact.headmasterQuote: owlproject.org raises the standard of living for children in these areas in 2 ways. It teaches them to nurture. They learn to look after the owls in their care, something not generally experienced by township children. Secondly, it teaches them awe and amazement for the world in which they live and the creatures with whom they share that world.
impact.description:
Owlproject.org was founded in 2001 with the purpose of introducing young South African children to the wonderful world of owls, their beauty as well as their enormous potential as partners in the control and management of rats within the often rodent infested and impoverished communities in which they live. In order to achieve this, it was essential to demystify the negative stigma attached to owls in Southern Africa.

20 years on, 260,000 children and their parents have participated in the owlproject.org programme. A simple question to many urban South African children regarding owls will be met with the instantaneous answer, 'they eat rats'. Many informal settlement schools now enjoy occupied owl boxes of their own and participate in owl pellet dissection programmes that contribute greatly to owl/prey data analysis.

The programme has been presented at 2 world owl conferences and was awarded the Birdlife Africa Award for Conservation as well as an award from the International Owl Centre in Houston, Minnesota. Owlproject.org is now underway with the continuation of this programme into other parts of South Africa as well as into our neighbouring African countries.

The cornerstone of this programme is educational, although social and economic consideration is vital for the programme's success. In Africa, with its kaleidoscope of problems, from poverty, corruption, political and social unrest, the maxim 'Without education there can be no conservation' could not be more true.

whyItMatters.title: Why This Matters
whyItMatters.content:
There are so many challenges facing the youth in our country that the idea of donating to an owl programme in townships may seem frivolous. There are big issues that donor funds are required to tackle - health, education, food security, safety and more. Although rodents in townships impact on food security, affect health and the owlproject.org programme is highly educational, a discussion with a headmaster at one of our participating schools was particularly insightful.

As he explained: owlproject.org teaches children to nurture and look after the owls in their care—something not generally experienced by township children. It also teaches them awe and amazement for the world in which they live and the creatures with whom they share that world. These lessons create lasting positive impacts on children's relationship with nature and their environment.
